events.excerpt:
How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World

Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models.

Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world.

I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle.

As we’re still in the early days of building applications with foundation models, it’s normal to make mistakes. This is a quick note with examples of some of the most common pitfalls that I’ve seen, both from public case studies and from my personal experience.

Because these pitfalls are common, if you’ve worked on any AI product, you’ve probably seen them before.

1. Use generative AI when you don't need generative AI

Every time there’s a new technology, I can hear the collective sigh of senior engineers everywhere: “Not everything is a nail.” Generative AI isn’t an exception — its seemingly limitless capabilities only exacerbate the tendency to use generative AI for everything.

A team pitched me the idea of using generative AI to optimize energy consumption. They fed a household’s list of energy-intensive activities and hourly electricity prices into an LLM, then asked it to create a schedule to minimize energy costs. This piece overviews how black-box distillation works in practice to inform proposed legislation and ongoing policy debates around adversarial distillation. We consider how adversarial distillation from proprietary U.S. models may have occurred at each step of the process and highlight areas of uncertainty around the methods Chinese labs employed. We also consider the potential impact of that distillation on China’s AI development.

The post How Black-Box Distillation Works appeared first on Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

events.excerpt: ## New Models ### Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk) Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's largest and most capable model to date: a 1 trillion-parameter natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 49 billion active parameters per token (52 billion including embeddings and output layers), trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral's own datacenters in Europe. Mistral Large 4 unifies instruction following, reasoning, coding, and agentic workflows in a single set of weights. While a generalist model, it shows especially good performance on workloads such as cybersecurity, finance, and law, and it surpasses frontier closed models on visual grounding. events.excerpt:
# v0.32.0

## Highlights

This release features 814 commits from 363 contributors (121 new)!

* **Structured decisions and generic parsers**: the new `POST /v1/systemone` endpoint answers `choice`, `noul` and `score` questions over a structured state (#59299), is served by default (#60677, #60696), and also runs on `Cloudflare/clef-omni` (#61064), `LiquidAI/d1-3B` (#60676) and DiffusionGemma (#60466). The new `hf` tool and reasoning parser (`--tool-call-parser hf`, `--reasoning-parser hf`) reads the checkpoint's `response_template`, so models that ship it need no model-specific parser (#58604, #58602), in both the Python and Rust frontends (#59005).
* **Low-precision KV cache everywhere**: NVFP4 KV cache now runs on SM8x and SM12x (#46963), SM90 (#60620) and with XQA decode on SM12x (#60452), and on MiniMax-M3 sparse attention on SM100 (#59300); GLM-5.x defaults to an FP8 KV cache on SM100, halving KV memory per rank with 2.3-5.5% more throughput at a 7-11% TTFT cost in the PR's benchmark (#60140, #60281); `fp8_ds_mla` on SM90 gives GLM-5.3-Flash up to 31% more output throughput (#59246); ROCm gains the 4-bit `ultraquant_4bit` KV cache with about 2x the density of FP8 (#5705
